data.title: Court Says Rohingya Must Be Compensated; Tech Stocks Rise
data.description:
The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.

In an historic ruling, the ICJ ordered that the refugees must be given safe passage home and awarded compensation.

The ruling by the top UN court was the first time in its 80-year history that ICJ judges have determined that a state committed genocide, and is likely to be seen as justice for Rohingya victims of Myanmar’s brutal 2017 crackdown.

 

ALSO SEE: APEC Leaders in China; Thai Court Shuts Builder Tied to Collapse

 

Analysts said the ruling is an enormous setback with potentially severe implications for the Myanmar military and coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, including major financial repercussions if it fails to respect the judgement.

Indeed, it has been a rocky week for the former senior general, who reportedly took a swipe at both China and Thailand, which have both sought to normalise ties with their troubled neighbour, according to Irrawaddy News, after Myanmar was banned from attending the 49th ASEAN summit.

The coup leader said he would review relations with ASEAN, claiming the regional grouping had taken an unreasonable position in regard to Myanmar.

However, ASEAN nations have been concerned about the huge humanitarian suffering after five years of bitter civil conflict, with the military still pounding civilian populations with regular aerial strikes on communities anywhere near fighting in states all over the country. More than 100,000 people have been killed and the economy ravaged.

 

Emotions run high after strong ruling

Thursday’s ruling was an answer to Rohingya prayers that surprised even some of the refugees’ biggest supporters.

ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa spelt out the verdict in the court’s Great Hall of Justice in The Hague, saying: “The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State.”

The court ordered Myanmar to launch a probe into anyone suspected of carrying out genocide during its 2017 crackdown against the Rohingya.

Myanmar “must take immediate and effective steps to investigate all persons reasonably suspected of having committed acts (of genocide)… and if warranted, to prosecute and punish them,” the court president said.

“Myanmar is under an obligation to compensate the Rohingya group and its members for the damage caused by the violations of its obligations… in so far as such damage is not made good by restitution.”

In Cox’s Bazar, now the world’s biggest refugee camp, hundreds followed proceedings from The Hague on a giant screen, many breaking down in tears when Iwasawa pronounced the verdict of genocide.

Mohammed Osman, whose parents and four siblings were killed by the Myanmar military, said the verdict had proved that “we were not lying about the genocide”.

“I am overwhelmed … But we have achieved only 50% of what we wanted. We will achieve 100% when we are repatriated with dignity,” Osman, 20, told AFP.

For nearly three hours, Iwasawa laid out searing evidence of Myanmar’s atrocities against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority during the campaign, which forced hundreds of thousands to flee into neighbouring Bangladesh.

Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed “widespread sexual violence” against women and “extreme violence” against children, Iwasawa said.

The ICJ said the evidence pointed to around 10,000 killed in Myanmar’s so-called “clearance operations” to repress the Rohingya community.

Rohingya villages were “systemically destroyed” and replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, said the ICJ, ruling that the “only reasonable inference” was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population – a key test for genocide.

 

‘Safe’ return

The court ordered Myanmar to “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return to their place of residence” for those who fled the violence. UN chief Antonio Guterres swiftly called on Myanmar to allow that to happen.

Judges also told Myanmar it must investigate and punish anyone suspected of committing genocide, providing for compensation to be determined at a later date.

While the decisions of the ICJ are binding and cannot be appealed, the court has no way of enforcing its verdicts, and it remains to be seen whether Myanmar’s rulers will adhere to the orders.

But the ruling will likely heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing. He commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.

This year, he was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy – which may be badly undermined by the ruling.

The diplomatic reverberations were immediate, with Britain saying it would expel Myanmar’s defence attache in the wake of the verdict.

The watershed ICJ judgment was also being closely watched by legal experts for clues into how the court will rule in another high-profile case before it – whether Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.

The ruling provides “a significant precedent for victims of genocide, and other grave crimes, across the world in their own quest for justice,” said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch.

‘They survived’

The case was brought by The Gambia under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, which allows any state to bring a case against another it suspects of breaching the international agreement set up after World War II.

The African country’s justice minister told reporters at the court the verdict was a victory for the Rohingya, who had suffered great hardships.

“They survived. They testified. And today, they will believe,” said Dawda Jallow.

Myanmar had always denied genocide, arguing that its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

“Myanmar was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free rein,” its representative Ko Ko Hlaing told judges during hearings on the case in January.

There was no immediate reaction from the Myanmar authorities.

A Rohingya activist in Yangon said they were “really satisfied” by the decision, but feared potential blowback against the community still in Myanmar.

 

Trilateral fizzer

The ICJ verdict overshadowed the trilateral ‘summit’ in Shenzhen between Presidents Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump, which had been hailed by the hosts as a ground-breaking event, but yielded little in the way of outcomes, as many analysts had suspected.

China, the US and Russia issued a peace declaration after meeting for 80 minutes. They emerged saying they wanted to reform the United Nations, to protect diplomatic immunity and boost supply and production of refined petroleum products.

“The three heads of state engaged in an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed themselves to upholding strategic stability and international security,” said the statement published by Chinese state media and the Kremlin, but not yet by the White House, AFP reported.

Little appeared to have been achieved in terms of cutting nuclear weapons.

Critics warned that the optics from the meeting would be damaging for the US president – but a fillip to Xi and Putin.
The meeting “gives Putin a platform to legitimise his war of aggression over Ukraine with seemingly little repercussions,” said Lyle Morris at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

“Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin are playing Donald Trump like a cheap violin,” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said.

 

Anthropic lifts tech stocks

Meanwhile, technology shares mostly rose on Thursday as AI titan Anthropic prepares to start trading following its record IPO, which gives investors a chance to bet directly on the prospects for the maker of the hugely successful Claude models.

In a highly anticipated initial public offering on Wednesday, Anthropic priced its shares at $83 each, raising more than $80 billion – topping Elon Musk’s SpaceX’s blockbuster stock sale in June.

That values the company at around $1.5 trillion ahead of the start of trading in its shares on the Nasdaq later Thursday.

The news reinforced optimism that was hammered last week after the shock resignation of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang over his extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The scandal rocking the chip giant has compounded concerns about the eye-watering sums pumped into the AI buildout and when they will see a profit, if at all.

Traders have also been spooked by the US move to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s powerful AI chips remotely, adding to worries that a new Democratic-led Congress will impose further regulations.

In Asia tech stocks closed mostly higher, and Europe’s main equity indices advanced in midday deals.

Seoul and Tokyo, home to most of Asia’s leading AI-linked firms, rose after a rocky couple of weeks, with chip giants SK Hynix, Samsung, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron all markedly higher.

But stocks in Taiwan slumped as investors eyed the trilateral summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, against a backdrop of fears about a Chinese takeover of the island. Hong Kong also closed lower.

Elsewhere, oil prices edged higher after the International Energy Agency said the crisis in the Middle East had created the “largest threat” to energy security in history.

The agency said in its annual World Energy Outlook that consumers were increasingly footing the bill as the world runs out of ways to absorb the impact of the conflict on energy supplies.

 

  • Jim Pollard with Agence France-Presse

data.title: China Warns The US as New Tariff Push Upsets Allies And Foes
data.description:
China warned on Thursday that it would take “necessary measures” after Washington unveiled new tariffs that risk shaking the uneasy truce in the countries’ trade war that expires on January 10.

China was one of a raft of countries, which also include major economies such as Europe and Japan, that the Trump Administration is proposing to hit with hefty levies of up to 20%.

Announcing the proposed levies for a raft of countries on Wednesday, Washington set the rate at 20% for China but warned it could double to 40%.

 

ALSO SEE: Huawei Found Guilty in Trade, Fraud Case; China Warns on Tariffs

 

“China urges the United States to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” Chinese commerce ministry spokesman He Yadong said.

“China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests,” He told a regular briefing.

US President Donald Trump has long criticised China’s yawning trade surplus with the United States, blaming it for a decline in local manufacturing prowess and jobs.

In his second term, Trump has slapped new tariffs on Chinese goods, kicking off a tit-for-tat escalation that at one point saw some duties touch 145%.

The trade ceasefire struck by Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in October 2025 was extended by two months in September until January 10.

Beijing agreed to buy more US soybeans and other agricultural products, and to suspend rare earths restrictions for a year.

 

Greer: ‘China understands’

Tensions are beginning to show, however, with both sides complaining about recent actions by the other.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told his Chinese counterpart this month that “continued progress depends on concrete results and that the United States will closely assess China’s implementation of the arrangement”, according to a statement.

Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in response expressed “serious concerns over recent economic and trade restrictive measures imposed by the United States”, according to state media.

Trump and Xi met last week at a regional summit in Shenzhen in southern China and are due to see each other for the fourth time this year in December at a G20 summit in the United States.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing.

“China understands that we’re going to have some level of tariffs. This falls within that understanding,” he told US broadcaster CNBC, adding that Washington was offering Beijing exemptions on around $30 billion of goods.

 

Usual pattern

The escalation in tariffs is “not a surprise to China”, Dan Wang, a director on Eurasia Group’s China team, told AFP.

“It has become a pattern before every major top leader summit,” Wang said, adding that she did not think the new measures would derail relations between Washington and Beijing.

“Xi has a high incentive to keep bilateral relations stable leading up to the 21st (Communist) Party congress in October” 2027, said Wang.

The latest tariff proposals mark the “third big action” recently affecting relations between Washington and Beijing, Alicia Garcia-Herrero, Asia-Pacific chief economist at Natixis, told AFP.

The first was the tumultuous scandal enveloping US chip titan Nvidia and its boss Jensen Huang, whose extramarital affair with a woman accused of spying for China contributed to his removal – before a sudden return – as chief executive.

The second, she said, was the conviction on Tuesday by a US jury of Chinese tech giant Huawei for stealing trade secrets, an outcome slammed by Beijing as “suppressing” companies from the country.

 

Probe into excess production

Analysts say the new US tariffs, after Washington concluded its months-long probe into alleged excess production, have the potential to open a new phase in trade tensions with both allies and foes alike.

The new tolls, which follow an investigation launched days after the Supreme Court struck down President Donald Trump’s previous duties, range up to 20% and face a period of public comment before taking effect, at the earliest in January.

The levies target some of the United States’ largest trading partners, with China, the European Union, India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam in the crosshairs.

Some, such as Japan, denied having excessive production.

“Japan does not have any non-market policy practices or structural excess production capacity… It is regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced in spite of this,” the country’s top government spokesman Minoru Kihara said.

A senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, noted that the proposals sought to take existing trade deals into account.

China is among those facing a 20% tariff, but US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing.

He told US broadcaster CNBC, adding that Washington was offering China exemptions on around $30 billion of goods.

 

US should stick to deal: EU

The European Union said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected the United States to stick by a deal struck last year.

“The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said.

And Singapore said on Thursday it was “very disappointed” with the proposals and denied it was protecting its domestic market or subsidizing manufacturing.

Vietnam also faces a 20% tariff; Cambodia and Indonesia 18%; and India 17%, according to the USTR’s office.

The EU, South Korea and Taiwan, which have signed trade deals with the United States, will see tariffs broadly capped at 15%.

In a separate announcement, the USTR also proposed additional tariffs on goods from Brazil, including aircraft, over alleged inaction on addressing US trade concerns.

The Brazilian president’s office called the measures “unacceptable” and said Brasilia would “not yield to this type of threat.”

Trump’s tariffs have targeted Washington’s friends and foes alike, and are part of a push in his second term to remake global trade by forcing countries to buy US products or produce their goods in the country.

Overcapacity concerns affect a range of sectors, from batteries to cement and chemicals to processed food, the senior US official said.

data.title: Huawei Found Guilty in Trade, Fraud Case; China Warns on Tariffs
data.description:
Tensions between the US and China rose on Wednesday after a US jury found tech giant Huawei guilty of stealing trade secrets and lying to regulators over its dealings in Iran.

Huawei, which is now the world’s top equipment manufacturer, was found guilty on 10 counts – including bank fraud and conspiracy to defraud the United States – after a three-month hearing in a New York Federal Court.

The verdict led to Beijing claiming that the United States was “suppressing” its companies. But it also warned the US against imposing new tariffs on China and other countries.

 

ALSO SEE: US Aims at Chip Smuggling; Markets Jump on Huang’s Return

 

The ruling comes at a politically sensitive time for the United States and China, whose leaders sought to project what Trump called a “fantastic” relationship when they met in Shenzhen last week.

China hit back after the court ruling, saying it “firmly opposes the US suppressing and containing Chinese enterprises and firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests.”

Trump’s administration has long alleged a risk of Huawei spying on behalf of the Chinese government, and previously urged countries not to use the company’s infrastructure in new 5G mobile networks.

“No person or company is above the law,” US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement after the conviction.

“For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft.”

Huawei rejected the conviction on Wednesday, saying in a statement it was “without legal or factual merit. We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests,” it added.

 

Acquitted on 2 charges

The jury did, however, acquit Huawei of racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice, a move the company said it “welcomed,” adding that it “confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years.”

The charges in part involved Huawei’s business dealings with the government of Iran.

“Huawei repeatedly lied about the nature of its business in Iran, falsely telling banks, journalists, and the US government that it did not assist Iran’s government, military, or intelligence community,” the DOJ said.

“Huawei lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of US dollars and access to US-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services – in part because of its lies.”

The equipment manufacturer was also accused of attempting to recruit employees of US telecoms firms and obtaining technological information from them in the process.

That data allegedly enabled Huawei to develop products similar to those of its competitors, which it then sold at lower prices, according to the original indictment.

“The misappropriated intellectual property included trade secret information and copyrighted works, such as source code and user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology, and robot testing technology,” the DOJ said in a release.

Huawei even launched an internal programme offering bonuses to employees who obtained industrial secrets from competitors, prosecutors claimed.

“Today’s verdict sends an unmistakable message: America will defend its businesses, protect its workers, and safeguard its national security against corrupt foreign corporations that lie, cheat, and steal to get ahead,” Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva said in a statement.

 

New levies

Meanwhile, Beijing urged the United States to “uphold the stable development” of trade relations, after media reports said Washington was planning to announce new tariffs on China and other countries.

The reports said that Washington’s new levies would affect major US trading partners, including China, the European Union, Japan and South Korea.

“Tariff wars and trade wars are not in anyone’s interest,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said, when asked about Washington’s reported plans.

He told a regular briefing that the world’s two top economies, which in 2025 agreed a tenuous truce in their trade war, “should resolve relevant issues through consultation”.

He added that accusations of overcapacity – mass production at a loss to flood overseas markets and undercut local rivals – was a “false premise” and a “pretext for political manipulation”.

“China and the United States should work together to effectively implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state and uphold the stable development of China-US economic and trade relations,” he said.

President Donald Trump has long criticised China’s yawning trade surplus with the United States, which he has blamed for a decline in local manufacturing prowess and jobs.

After starting a second term in office last year, Trump imposed new tariffs on Chinese goods, kicking off a tit-for-tat escalation with Beijing that at one point saw duties soar as high as 145%.

The trade ceasefire struck by Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in October 2025 is due to expire in January, after a two-month extension was agreed in September.

The two men met last week at an APEC summit in Shenzhen in southern China and are due to see each other again in December at a G20 summit in the United States.

During their meeting at APEC, which came just before a historic trilateral with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Xi hailed China’s “stable and improved” ties with the United States.

The Chinese leader also said that his country should cooperate in the field of artificial intelligence, keeping the technology “under human control” and guarding against safety risks.

data.title: US Aims at Chip Smuggling; Markets Jump on Huang’s Return
data.description:
Singapore’s prime minister vowed on Tuesday to cooperate with the United States after it added the company at the centre of the Nvidia scandal to a trade backlist, after CEO Jensen Huang’s stunning return to the helm of the US chip giant.

Huang resigned over extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, an executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed International, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

News of his return sent Nvidia shares soaring 31.5% and pulled the tech-heavy Nasdaq up more than 6%.

 

ALSO SEE: Oil States Blamed For Climate Talks Collapse; Tech Sell-off in Asia

 

The company said on Monday that it had reinstated Huang as chief executive after receiving information from the US government that he did not pose a national security risk. US President Donald Trump reportedly lobbied the board for Huang to be reinstated.

Following Huang’s return, the US added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist that bars it from purchasing advanced chips.

The company, along with four affiliates in Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, was added to the US Commerce Department’s Entity List for “acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States” on Monday, the department said in a filing on the Federal Register.

Singapore-based Apex Enterprise Solutions, a subsidiary of Chinese tech giant Alibaba, was also added to the list.

The move prompted Malaysia to urge data centre operators to cut links with seven companies, including Megaspeed and two local firms on the blacklist.

Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said on Tuesday the city-state did not want to be “used and abused by companies” to get around US export controls on high-end chips.

He said his country was working with the US to stop companies “exploiting Singapore’s position to tranship and reroute chips through Singapore to other parts of Southeast Asia or to other countries”.

 

Trump says he spoke to Nvidia board

US President Donald Trump said Huang’s return followed his own direct contacts with Nvidia’s board, calling it a “correct and proper decision”.

“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” he told CNBC.

Huang has developed a close relationship with Trump since his return to the White House, joining him on foreign trips and negotiating directly with the administration over chip exports to China.

The board voted unanimously to bring Huang back as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately, the company said in a statement.

It said that input from “senior levels” of the US government had left it confident his return posed no national security risk, without naming the officials.

Board chair Harvey Jones said directors believe Huang “is the right person to lead Nvidia.”

Jones will remain chair, and chief financial officer Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, will continue as CFO.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said in the statement. “I can’t wait to get back to work.”

Employees at Nvidia cheered as Huang returned to the office, according to videos posted by staff.

“Thank you all for the second chance,” Huang said. “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”

Huang had offered to return after stepping down on November 12, but Jones told investors on an earnings call last week that directors did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”.

His comeback followed a campaign by Silicon Valley figures, including Elon Musk, while thousands of current and former Nvidia employees signed an open letter calling for his reinstatement.

 

Huang to testify next week

It comes after reports that the 63-year-old CEO had an affair with a former executive at Megaspeed, a company that bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips.

Media reports subsequently revealed another alleged affair with an Nvidia subordinate.

US intelligence services have reportedly concluded that Alice Huang passed information to Beijing, which has denied the allegations.

A committee of independent directors investigating whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort will complete its probe, Nvidia said on Monday, without giving further details.

Huang is due to testify to US lawmakers behind closed doors next week and faces further scrutiny when Democrats take control of Congress in January.

House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries called the board’s decision “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible”, and said Congress would not be deterred from a “swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation” of Nvidia.

The scandal exposed divisions within Trump’s administration over Huang and China, with hawks accusing the Commerce Department of failing to police Nvidia’s chip sales to Beijing.

Huang’s departure sent Wall Street tumbling and stoked fears for a US economy reliant on the AI investment boom, before global stocks surged upon his return.

 

Tech stocks jump

Technology firms rocketed on Tuesday as Asia joined a global stock surge following the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia boss.

The Silicon Valley giant’s resignation on November 12 sent shockwaves through markets and dealt a severe blow to the AI trade, which was already under pressure amid worries over profitability and the vast sums pumped into the sector.

Huang’s role as a fixer and visionary in an industry that has fuelled a tech revolution and a global economic boom was seen as crucial to the firm’s future, as well as the AI buildout.

News of his return – announced soon after the opening bell on Monday – lit a fire under equities, sending shares in Nvidia soaring by 31.5% and added more than $900 billion to the firm’s market value.

Other Wall Street titans also enjoyed much-needed buying, pulling the Nasdaq up more than 6%, the S&P 500 4.7% and the Dow 3%.

And then Asia, which had started the week on the back foot, followed suit.

 

Global rally

Taipei was the standout, blasting 9% higher as chip titans TSMC and MediaTek added nearly 10% each. Seoul piled on more than 6% thanks to strong gains in market heavyweights SK hynix and Samsung.

Tokyo ended up close to 4% thanks to spikes of 12.5% in Advantest, 7.7% in Tokyo Electron and 10% in Kioxia.

Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington, Bangkok and Manila also joined in the fun. However, Hong Kong edged down as Chinese tech firms failed to take advantage of the global rally.

“Jensen’s return takes away one of the biggest unknowns hanging over the AI trade,” said Saxo Markets’ Charu Chanana.

“He is not just Nvidia’s CEO; he is arguably the biggest salesman for the entire AI ecosystem. His relationships with customers, suppliers and capital providers are difficult to replicate.

“(His) return is particularly welcome for Asian technology stocks, many of which suffered collateral damage from Nvidia’s leadership crisis.”

 

Alice Huang ‘in contact with spy agency’

National Australia Bank’s Gavin Friend said: “The AI trade has been given a reprieve, with Huang’s reinstatement assuaging fears of any unravelling of the circular financing activity that has been a key support for the sector.”

However, analysts added that Huang’s reinstatement did not mean an end to probes or the uncertainty that has clouded the AI trade for the past six months.

The company is still under scrutiny from investigators at the FBI and on Capitol Hill.

Huang reportedly had a relationship with Alice Huang (no relation) – a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. The group is under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese firms gain access to Nvidia’s top-line chips.

Just this weekend, the New York Times added further details to the allegations, saying Alice Huang had been in touch with China’s top spy agency during the secret affair.

The United States added Megaspeed on Monday to a trade blacklist that bars it from purchasing advanced chips.

Oil prices continued to fall after Monday’s sharp drop that saw WTI back below $80 for the first time since August.

The latest selling was fuelled by hopes for an end to the Iran conflict as Axios reported US Vice President JD Vance met the prime minister of Qatar, which has acted as a mediator in efforts to resolve the nine-month conflict.

data.title: Oil States Blamed For Climate Talks Collapse; Tech Sell-off in Asia
data.description:
Anger and frustration lingered in Turkey on Monday after the COP31 climate summit collapsed in a bitter dispute over the mention of fossil fuels.

Climate advocates blamed petro-states such as Saudi Arabia for the failure to agree on a statement after the meeting in Antalya stretched into record overtime.

The final agreement was rejected on Sunday in a chaotic finale to the UN climate summit that ran two days over schedule, underscoring the strains on diplomacy in an increasingly fractured world.

 

ALSO SEE: Asia Stocks Worst Week in 5 Years, Indon Fire Losses Near $30bn

 

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, who urged nations to send fossil fuels “the way of the dinosaurs” during a fiery appearance at the talks, expressed deep dismay.

“I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands,” the outgoing UN chief said in a statement.

COP31 negotiations chair Chris Bowen, who sought unsuccessfully to broker consensus among nearly 200 nations, conceded he could not overcome what he called “unbridgeable red lines”.

“Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision… And that’s disappointing. Very disappointing,” Bowen, who is Australia’s climate minister, told a throng of reporters.

More than 49 hours after the summit was supposed to end, COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum banged the gavel to conclude the marathon talks.

 

Oil states reject any mention of cutting fossil fuels

Bowen said the summit backdrop was “the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory”, as soaring energy prices and fallout from the Middle East war complicated the search for unity.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the summit with Turkey, attributed the failure of the talks to “difficult geopolitical times”.

Under pressure to show progress in a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Nepal, Bowen sought an overarching “cover decision” to prove countries were still united in tackling the crisis.

But his plan unravelled as familiar fault lines emerged over fossil fuels, with the EU and Saudi Arabia locking horns over the pace of the shift away from coal, oil and gas.

The negotiations stalled as oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels in the final deal.

“We will not endorse a cover decision… that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change,” said Ireland’s climate minister, Darragh O’Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency.

“And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel.”

Panama, Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands also objected and as the deal imploded, COP31 became the longest climate summit on record.

Former US vice president and climate advocate Al Gore said it was “outrageous that a handful of petrostates have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels”.

The COP process is “in need of significant reform”, Gore said on X, as most countries sought “to move forward in good faith.”

 

COP may be scrapped

The outcome revived memories of the failed Copenhagen summit of 2009 and raised fresh doubts about the effectiveness of climate diplomacy.

“It certainly fell short today,” UN climate chief Simon Stiell said. “The world cannot afford a repeat.”

Frustrated by the inertia, countries are pushing ahead outside the COP process.

Around 60 countries joined a first-of-its-kind conference in April on phasing out fossil fuels, while several nations at COP31 unveiled their own plans to exit coal, oil and gas.

In a last-ditch bid for compromise, COP31 co-hosts Turkey and Australia could only muster a veiled reference to fossil fuels in the final text.

But the pact also took fire for retaining a call to expand carbon capture – a costly technology championed by the fossil fuel industry that critics say is expensive and offers limited impact.

“We believe that climate change requires all solutions on the table,” said Mohammad Ayoub, a climate negotiator for oil giant Saudi Arabia.

Facing blowback over the fossil fuels omission, the co-host nations tried to rally support behind a global goal to electrify the world economy.

They said “electrification” could cut heat-trapping emissions and bolster energy security but the target was ultimately torpedoed, along with the rest of the doomed Antalya Pact.

Push for climate finance dies

Countries lamented a missed opportunity to reinforce the Paris agreement’s 1.5C target, which scientists expect the world to overshoot in a few years as carbon-cutting goals fall short.

The summit also widened fault lines over science, with a fight over the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) spilling into the negotiations.

“We are profoundly disappointed by the substance of the cover decision,” UK climate negotiator Kate Hughes said.

“It moves us backwards on the science… It is a lowest common denominator where it should have been, instead, presenting bold collective ambition on climate action.”

As always, the summit laid bare the divide between major polluters driving climate change and smaller nations bearing the brunt of its impact.

Developing nations pushed for a $120 billion target climate goal, which disappeared from the failed deal.

 

Asian tech sell-off continues

Asian stock markets struggled to recover from last week’s sell-off, with tech firms again in the firing line as investors tracked an eye-watering rout on Wall Street.

A healthy bounce in US futures was unable to inspire buying amid fears over the AI trade, the prospect of more Federal Reserve interest rate hikes and tighter regulation under a Democrat-led Congress.

Scandal-hit Nvidia characterised the collapse in New York on Friday, plunging 14% and helping to drag the Nasdaq into negative territory for the year.

The index has lost almost a fifth of its value since hitting a record high just last month, with strong earnings from Nvidia and a blockbuster IPO from Claude-creator Anthropic unable to staunch the bloodletting.

The selling continued into Asia, with Seoul diving more than 5% as chip titans SK Hynix and Samsung were hammered again.

“These are not peripheral players in the AI boom but two of its most important semiconductor suppliers,” SPI Asset Management’s Stephen Innes said.

“Their continued weakness suggests investors are still more interested in reducing exposure than celebrating a few hours of improved sentiment in US futures.”

The losses have led authorities in some countries to introduce measures aimed at minimising the negative impact.

Taiwan was making it harder to short stocks, while China made it easier to borrow money to buy them and South Korea eyed a stabilisation fund not used since the global financial crisis.

Taipei benefited from the moves, ending up more than 2% as TSMC and MediaTek spiked, while Shanghai, Manila and Jakarta also advanced.

But Hong Kong, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington, Mumbai and Bangkok all dropped into negative territory.

Tokyo was closed for a holiday.

Meanwhile, the VIX Index — which is seen as the market’s fear gauge – spiked to its highest level since April last year, when Donald Trump unveiled his wide-ranging tariff bazooka.

Traders have also been spooked by the US Commerce Department’s move to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s powerful AI chips remotely.

Fiona Cincotta at Forex.com said “nerves have been showing in the AI trade, amid increased scrutiny over AI capital expenditure, the scale of investment, the returns on those investments and when they might materialise”.

data.title: Asia Stocks Worst Week in 5 Years, Indon Fire Losses Near $30bn
data.description:
Tech stocks in North Asia took a beating this week, despite the surge in demand for shares of Anthropic, which failed to ease concerns about the AI sector.

Tech-rich Seoul, Tokyo and Taipei led the losses on Friday. Analysts said Anthropic’s sparkling debut failed to rouse a recovery in sentiment towards the AI trade, as investors’ nerves had been frayed by crisis-hit Nvidia, as well as profitability and regulation.

After its record-breaking initial public offering, Claude-creator Anthropic soared 17% on its first day as ordinary investors sought to grab a piece of the new kid on the block.

 

ALSO SEE: Court Says Rohingya Must Be Compensated; Tech Stocks Rise

 

But the rally did nothing to drag other, more established firms higher as the uncertainty that has hung over the tech sector in recent months sapped confidence, sending Wall Street deep into the red.

Magnificent Seven members who led a scorching surge over the past two years continued a retreat that has characterised trade since the summer, as investors fret over AI profitability, eye-watering spending, rising borrowing costs and geopolitics.

Microsoft, Apple, Amazon and Tesla were all well down, along with Nvidia – which is battling to deal with the fallout from a spy scandal that has led to the resignation of pivotal leader Jensen Huang.

The losses continued on US futures markets, with Anthropic dropping more than 4%.

Traders have also been spooked by the US Commerce Department’s move to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s powerful AI chips remotely, adding to worries that a new Democratic-led Congress will impose further regulations.

 

Nikkei, Kospi and Taiex all sink

The selling followed through to Asia, where Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei – home to the region’s leading AI-linked firms – tumbled between 5% and 6.2%.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 was dragged by losses of 11% in Kioxia and 14.5% in tech investor SoftBank, while TSMC shed 4.8% and MediaTek tanked 10% as Taiwan’s main stock market was dragged more than 6% lower.

SK Hynix and Samsung took the brunt as South Korea’s Kospi dived more than 5%.

Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Bangkok, Jakarta and Manila also took a pummelling.

London, Paris and Frankfurt extended the losses at the open.

The flight from risk boosted the safe-haven yen, helped by a surge in Japanese inflation last month that stoked bets on another central bank interest rate hike.

US Treasuries were also boosted, with yields on most term lengths dropping. Yields fall as demand sends prices higher.

“With volatility elevated, equity futures breaking support and high-beta assets under pressure, traders will increasingly look for signs of capitulation, stabilisation or a catalyst capable of reversing sentiment,” Chris Weston at Pepperstone said.

“The risk is that selling becomes self-reinforcing. As volatility rises, risk limits tighten, leveraged positions are reduced and systematic strategies can add to the pressure.

“Whether Anthropic’s IPO proves to be a defining moment for the AI trade remains to be seen. For now, the immediate priority is watching how markets settle into the weekend and whether buyers can regain control next week.”

 

Nvidia probes being monitored

Investors are keeping tabs on developments in the Nvidia case as California announced it was investigating whether the firm misled the public and investors about its chips ending up in China, despite federal export controls.

Huang resigned last week after reports alleged he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with a woman named Alice Huang who is a suspected Chinese spy.

Alice Huang, who is no relation, is the former director of Megaspeed, a cloud computing company based in Singapore that was investigated by local officials in 2025 over potential export control violations.

Jensen Huang has agreed to attend a closed-door questioning session about national security issues with Congressional officials on December 1.

Oil prices rose on worries about fresh violence in the Middle East and after the International Energy Agency said the crisis in the Middle East had created the “largest threat” to energy security in history.

The IEA said in its annual World Energy Outlook that consumers were increasingly footing the bill as the world runs out of ways to absorb the impact of the conflict on energy supplies.

Indonesian fire crisis

Meanwhile, wildfires that tore through Indonesian forest and peatland areas this year could cost the Southeast Asian country more than $30 billion, the co-author of a study on the subject said on Friday.

Losses of physical assets and from disrupted economic activity alone would cost an estimated 340 trillion rupiah ($18.6 billion), according to new research by the Jakarta-based Center of Economic and Law Studies (CELIOS).

That was equal to about 2.7% of Indonesia’s GDP, the CELIOS report said.

It said additional health costs from acute respiratory infections caused by the wildfires on Indonesia’s Borneo, Sumatra and Papua islands could be as high as 225 trillion rupiah ($12.3 billion).

“There are also economic costs borne by the public, both directly and indirectly,” CELIOS director Nailul Huda, a co-author of the report, told AFP.

Wildfires have burned through 2.88 million hectares (7.1 million acres) so far in 2026, according to the Nusantara Atlas deforestation monitor – an area 18 times the size of London.

Indonesia experiences fires every dry season, but this year’s blazes have been particularly severe.

Researchers said last week that a strong El Nino weather phenomenon, climate change, deforestation and peatland drainage for mining and plantations have supercharged this year’s fire season.

The fires emitted a foul haze that made hundreds of thousands of people in Indonesia ill and drifted as far as Malaysia and Singapore.

data.title: New US Chip Rules Will Impact Southeast Asia, as Well as China
data.description:
China has condemned new restrictions on computer chip exports announced by the US and vowed to take “necessary measures” after the White House moved to close a loophole that was exposed by media scrutiny after the Nvidia ‘spy’ scandal.

The curbs were announced on Monday by the Bureau of Industry and Security, which is in charge of export controls.

The new rule, which takes effect in 90 days, will require data centres anywhere in the world to have a US licence to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies whose headquarters are in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.

 

ALSO SEE: Xi, Trump, Putin to Discuss ‘World Peace’; Asia Stocks Down

 

The rules also require licences to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries the US commerce department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips.

Beijing’s foreign ministry denounced the curbs on Tuesday.

“The US repeatedly overstretches the concept of national security, abusing export control measures,” ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a news briefing, vowing that China will “take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests”.

The country’s commerce ministry also expressed “firm opposition” to the new restrictions anda threatened to impose countermeasures.

 

Trump arrives in Manila

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump went directly to a meeting of the Quad security grouping shortly after arriving in Manila on Tuesday evening.

The US leader went straight to a summit with the leaders of India, Japan and Australia – Narendra Modi, Sanae Takaichi and Anthony Albanese – to discuss issues related to counterbalancing China’s regional influence.

He was then due to meet leaders of the 11 Southeast Asian nations in the ASEAN grouping, some of whom wanted to discuss trade deals, while others want reassurances about the new US policy on advanced computer chips.

The new rule by Washington stems from the crisis at Nvidia. The new restriction is likely to worry ASEAN members, such as Singapore and Malaysia, which were both linked to the transfer and use of high-end Nvidia chips by Chinese companies operating in the countries.

Companies shipping high-end chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will now require a special licence, as these countries, and Brazil, were said to represent a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of Nvidia chips to China.

 

Singapore tainted by chip scandal

Singapore is working to maintain its reputation as a trusted business hub, after being tainted by claims that Chinese companies such as Megaspeed International exploited a loophole to gain access to top-end AI chips despite US export restrictions.

A widening scandal sparked by an affair between Jensen Huang, until recently head of US chip titan Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy put a spotlight on the city-state’s position as a global crossroads for the advanced semiconductors that power artificial intelligence.

The United States says its controls on the export of powerful AI chips made by Nvidia are necessary to protect its national security.

The new US rule attempts to block not only illicit chip smuggling, but also the large grey market of Chinese firms renting computing power from data centres full of advanced Nvidia chips in third countries, often in Southeast Asia.

It follows explosive reports of Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, which Washington is investigating for the alleged transfer of Nvidia chips to China in circumvention of US rules.

The scandal “is obviously not a good look for Singapore”, Chong Ja Ian, a political scientist with the National University of Singapore, told AFP.

Singapore is also probing what Megaspeed was up to, but Chong said the city-state must strengthen regulatory oversight to avoid the perception of “systemic issues”.

The Nvidia case may make it harder “to maintain the reputation of being a clean business hub by simply dealing with individual cases, rather than putting more stringent regulations and laws in place,” he said.

 

US, Thailand sign trade statement

Meanwhile, President Trump and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul signed a joint statement on trade on Tuesday, with the American leader hailing a “victory for both countries” in ongoing negotiations.

A framework agreement was unveiled a year ago, on the same day Trump announced a short-lived ceasefire between Thailand and its neighbour Cambodia following deadly border clashes.

The United States is Thailand’s largest export market, with the Southeast Asian nation recording a surplus of $71.7 billion last year, according to US data.

“We’re going to do a lot of trade,” Trump told a news conference on the sidelines of a summit of leaders from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila.

“Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on US exports” and “remove substantial non-tariff barriers on American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol, and poultry,” Trump said.

Thailand will also buy “an estimated $2.6 billion in additional US agricultural products”, he added. “This is an incredible victory for both countries.”

Anutin said negotiators had “reached a substantial conclusion” in their talks on the final agreement on reciprocal trade.

“I am confident that the agreement will be ready for us to sign real soon,” Anutin said.

The two sides also agreed a non-binding memorandum outlining increased cooperation on trading rare earth minerals, which are vital to tech products and of which China is the world’s leading producer.

In July, Washington imposed tariffs of 12.5% on imports from Thailand, one of dozens of countries targeted in an investigation into forced labour.

Deputy spokeswoman Lalida Persvivatana told AFP it marked “significant progress” in negotiations on an agreement on reciprocal trade (ART).

“However, the signing is not yet the formal ART agreement,” she said, noting Thailand still needed to conduct a public consultation and legal procedures.

 

Protest over AI hub north of Manila

There is also a local issue – around 2,000 demonstrators staged a protest over environmental impacts from the Pax Silica initiative and plans for a 4,000-acre (1,620-hectare) economic security zone and AI industrial acceleration hub in New Clark City, about 100km north of Manila.

While the Quad has quietly progressed in deepening coordination, the short time allotted for Tuesday’s meeting meant it was unlikely to extend beyond pleasantries, Ryan Hass of the Brookings Institution told AFP.

The timing, however, carried significance, he said, given the historical meeting Trump will attend with the leaders of China and Russia in just two days.

“It’s a way of inoculating Trump against criticism of caving to authoritarians when he meets with Xi (Jinping) and (Vladimir) Putin in Shenzhen,” Hass said.

Hayley Channer, economic security director at the Sydney-based United States Studies Centre, said Trump’s decision to include ASEAN on his travel agenda was noteworthy.

“Southeast Asia has never been a high priority for the United States, so President Trump travelling to Manila is significant,” she added.

A spokesman for Japan’s foreign ministry said the Quad agenda would include discussions of the East and South China Sea — areas where multiple parties have overlapping claims with China.

Trump will later attend a meeting with ASEAN heads of state before going to a gala dinner.

While ASEAN leaders have spent three days grappling with a raft of regional issues, the spectre of Trump’s ongoing tariff blitz has loomed large.

 

Palace meet with Marcos

Trump is set to meet with Philippine leader Ferdinand Marcos at the presidential palace on Wednesday before heading to Shenzhen.

Channer, from the US Studies Centre, said while presidents routinely focus on foreign affairs as their terms wind down, Trump’s sit-down was “more likely because the US is trying to further its Pax Silica initiative, to build a complete mine-to-chip supply chain”.

Aimed at countering China’s dominance in semiconductors and rare earths, the initiative has been the focus of months of protests, as its flagship 1,620-hectare (about 4,000-acre) AI manufacturing hub north of Manila threatens to displace Indigenous families.

US Ambassador Lee Lipton, a Trump appointee, last week released a statement saying a long-rumoured deal signing for the site would not take place during the president’s visit.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Monday slammed what he called a “countercurrent of unilateralism and protectionism” while touting Beijing’s expanding trade with the bloc.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Canada’s Mark Carney sang a similar tune on trade, with both explicitly citing a need to wean themselves off dependence on the American market.

Meanwhile, US chip titan Nvidia said on Tuesday it had created an oversight committee for national security and export control in the wake of a spy scandal that forced chief Jensen Huang to quit.

“Nvidia today announced that the Board of Directors has established the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, a new standing committee responsible for board-level oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management,” the company said in a statement.

It was due to release its quarterly earnings late last night (Asia time).

data.title: China Fears More Curbs Amid Alice Huang’s ‘Suspect Chip Deals’
data.description:
China is worried that the scandal at US tech giant Nvidia – which saw its CEO Jensen Huang resign on Thursday over alleged extramarital affairs and espionage – will lead to tougher export controls on the company’s world-leading computer chips.

Beijing warned the United States on Friday not to impose additional curbs on chip exports.

Asked about calls from US lawmakers to impose more limits on chip equipment, foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular briefing that China “has consistently opposed the abuse of export control measures, which disrupts the stability of global industrial and supply chains and serves no party’s interests.”

 

ALSO SEE: Huang Resigns as Head of Nvidia, Kress Made Interim CEO

 

“China and the United States should work together to implement the important consensus reached by their respective heads of state and maintain the stable development of China-US economic and trade relations,” Mao said.

It’s been like that all week. On Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using spurious spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological “blockade” on China.

“China’s technological progress is driven by independent innovation and open cooperation. The US side should stop fabricating such ‘spy’ narratives as a pretext for imposing a technological blockade,” Mao said.

Jensen Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and global chip titan, stepped down on Thursday after admitting to an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.

That was the bombshell news of the week, which has put an intense media focus on both Jensen and Alice, who are not related, but also the Chinese woman’s suspect business dealings.

Reports allege that the Commerce Department under Secretary Howard Lutnick may have failed to act on suspicions that Megaspeed was helping to reroute restricted Nvidia chips to China.

US media quoted US lawmakers as saying they are in favour of imposing additional export controls on chips to China as a result of the snowballing scandal.

“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here. I’m in favour of limiting those exports,” House speaker Mike Johnson was quoted as saying.

“I think there is a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.”

US intelligence reportedly circulated a memo this spring alleging that Alice Huang was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security.

Beijing has rejected the allegations and said on Thursday they were a “pretext for imposing a technological blockade” to stop China advancing in artificial intelligence technology.

The furore comes ahead of a meeting expected next week between US President Donald Trump and Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Shenzhen in southern China at an APEC gathering.

 

US lawmakers summon Huang

Meanwhile, US lawmakers have called the former Nvidia CEO, who is a key architect of the AI boom, to face questioning in December over his dealings with Alice Huang, who US officials suspect was a Chinese spy.

The scandal has wiped almost half a trillion dollars off Nvidia’s market value, but their affair raised concern on whether Megaspeed, Alice Huang’s data centre firm in Singapore, was used to help Chinese companies such as Alibaba get access to advanced Nvidia chips, via a subsidiary in Malaysia, or directly into China.

“Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology,” Republican Senator Tim Scott wrote Thursday on X.

Scott said he was requesting Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify in December before the Senate Banking Committee, which he chairs.

It joins a call for a closed-door interview with the leather-jacketed, 63-year-old Huang on December 1 by three House of Representatives committees, on threat of subpoena, AFP reported.

US intelligence reportedly circulated a memo in spring this year alleging that Alice Huang was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Beijing has rejected that allegation.

On Wednesday, The New York Times reported a second affair, citing video of Huang being affectionate with Nvidia’s vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell.

Nvidia’s board announced late on Thursday that chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO, while it searches for a permanent successor to Huang, who spent 33 years at the helm of the firm he co-founded.

Nvidia hit gold when the launch of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in 2022 sparked a global rush to develop AI, with its processors – once designed for video game graphics – becoming a crucial ingredient to train and run the technology.

Huang, who was born in Taiwan, was a close informal adviser to President Donald Trump on AI, and had spent years lobbying against curbs on sales of advanced AI chips to China for national security reasons.

Singapore barred Chinese ‘spy’

Singapore said on Thursday it had barred Alice Huang, a Chinese national, from re-entering the country in February for giving investigators inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed, though she was not investigated for espionage.

Nvidia’s board opened a probe on Sunday into reporting that Huang had been the target of a “foreign intelligence effort,” while saying it retained confidence in him.

At the heart of the spy allegations is the race between the United States and China for supremacy in an industry widely seen as the next industrial revolution.

Singapore’s home ministry said it had repeatedly sought information from the US Justice Department and FBI on a US server supplier during its Megaspeed probe, but “received limited information or assistance.”

Malaysia also said on Friday that it was investigating a subsidiary of Megaspeed International over the possible diversion of advanced AI chips to other countries.

Alice Huang’s tangled corporate web

Singapore-based tech group Megaspeed dealt in billions of dollars’ worth of the world’s most advanced AI chips, but its office was an empty shell when AFP visited, its staff seemingly vanished long before claims of espionage landed at their door.

Details about Alice Huang’s life have been revealed by a range of media outlets. AFP said it is hard to pin down where she lives or works currently, but some suspect she is back in China.

Business filings in Singapore described her as a Chinese citizen with a Hong Kong passport.

She was born in China’s landlocked Hunan province, which she left to study media in Hong Kong, HK01 media reported.

Huang, now in her late 40s, did a master’s degree in media management at Hong Kong Baptist University in the late 2000s.

A CCTV reporter wrote on Weibo that she worked with Huang at the Chinese broadcaster, but later deleted the post, AFP reported.

A corporate CV published by a Chinese investment firm details her rapid ascent through the ranks of Asian investment banking.

She served in a senior role at HSBC sometime around 2012, the resume claims, before moving on to stints at CITIC Securities and Shanghai Hexi Investment.

She married Kang Wei, a Chinese businessman, who The Wall Street Journal said had met Jensen Huang through their mutual involvement in video game businesses.

In fact, the Journal said Kang “appeared to accept his wife’s romantic relationship with the Nvidia CEO and spoke openly of their closeness.”

AFP said corporate records filed in Hong Kong show that Alice Huang sits in the middle of a corporate web, connected to myriad shell companies, investment houses and major Chinese technology firms.

They list her as a director of Nanjing Lingxing Technology, which operates the popular T3 ride-hailing platform in China.

Other notable investors in Nanjing Lingxing Technology include Alibaba and Tencent, as well as state-backed carmakers like China FAW and Dongfeng Motor Group.

 

Megaspeed linked to chip deals

Megaspeed touts itself as a company at the heart of the AI revolution, using Nvidia’s advanced silicon chips to power high-performance computing inside vast data centres.

But it is also under investigation for serving a murkier purpose. Under the guise of buying computer hardware for its Southeast Asia data hubs, Megaspeed allegedly helped Beijing skirt trade restrictions by sending Nvidia chips into China.

Beijing has denied allegations of spying, and Megaspeed said it was investigating if it had complied with export controls on the sensitive chips, AFP said.

At Megaspeed’s office in the heart of the Singapore business district, no staff could be seen behind its locked glass doors. Neighbours told AFP they had not seen anyone come or go for the past few months.

Likewise in a mall at a newly developed neighbourhood in Johor, the Malaysian region a bridge away from Singapore, no employees were around in subsidiary Speedmatrix’s office.

Singapore police opened an investigation in February 2025 into Megaspeed and several other companies suspected of circumventing or violating export controls.

Alice Huang was interviewed as part of Singapore’s probe. Although no charges were laid, she was barred from the city-state in February 2026 for providing inaccurate information to “downplay her role in Megaspeed”, Singapore’s home ministry said.

 

Records show huge jump in income

Corporate records show Huang’s direct involvement in the birth of Megaspeed. A company linked to her acquired the Singapore arm of Chinese video game developer 7Road International in early 2023.

Almost immediately, the 7Road name was changed to Megaspeed International. Alice Huang was listed as a Megaspeed director for less than a year, taking the role between March and November 2023.

Her arrival coincided with a drastic change in fortunes, as Megaspeed pivoted from a little-known video game-maker to one of Asia’s biggest buyers of Nvidia chips.

Within 12 months, Megaspeed’s revenue jumped from $0 to almost $300 million, according to company accounts filed in 2024.

Megaspeed – which described itself as a “cloud hosting services provider” – saw the value of its assets skyrocket from $32 million to almost $3 billion over the same period.

Just one of Nvidia’s advanced AI computer chips can cost tens of thousands of dollars. And over two years, Megaspeed reportedly traded in upwards of $4 billion worth of Nvidia chips.

A financial trail weaving through Singapore, Malaysia and the Cayman Islands suggests Megaspeed’s business may have been boosted by a connection to Chinese tech giant Alibaba, AFP said.

Megaspeed has a Malaysian subsidiary that struck a deal in 2024, pledging assets to Apex Enterprise Solutions in Singapore as security in case of contractual breaches.

Apex is linked through a parent company to Alibaba Group Holding Ltd, a firm registered in the Cayman Islands, Singapore corporate data shows.

By that time, Huang was no longer registered as a director at Megaspeed. But Singapore authorities said she remained one of Megaspeed’s “key controllers”.

Megaspeed’s ultimate holding company is a Singapore firm called Swiftdata.

 

Awkward questions

In June 2025, US investigators turned up at Megaspeed to carry out a “post-shipment verification”, with Huang present, according to Singapore’s home ministry, adding that it was the first time it found out about Washington’s probe.

On the same day, Huang was interviewed by Singapore police, who impounded her passport. By then, she and Nvidia boss Jensen Huang had already been spotted together in public.

In one of their early outings together, they were seen mingling at a party after the Computex trade show in Taiwan at the beginning of 2024.

Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about their relationship well before it exploded into a public scandal, but said Sunday he did not regret not acting on it.

“No, I don’t think so. I think – you know, he’s an honorable guy,” Trump said.

But with China and the United States fighting for supremacy in artificial intelligence, Nvidia’s market-leading products have become a major point of contention.

Nvidia controls an estimated 90% of the market for the chips used to train and run AI models, and the US imposed rules in 2022 to restrict their sales to China.

A Chinese university tied to the nation’s defence establishment was able to buy advanced Nvidia chips, according to procurement notices from October and September.

Singapore’s probe into Megaspeed is ongoing. And Malaysia said on Friday it’s also investigating the company’s subsidiary Speedmatrix to determine if chips imported into the country had been exported to other jurisdictions.

Megaspeed itself said it has retained a US law firm to examine its compliance.

“Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously,” it said.

data.title: Huang Resigns as Head of Nvidia, Kress Made Interim CEO
data.description:
Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive of AI giant Nvidia on Thursday after it was revealed he had two extramarital affairs, one of them with a woman accused of spying for China.

The chief financial officer at the world’s second biggest company, Colette Kress, will act as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor, the company said.

The announcement, late on Thursday Asia time, ends Huang’s 33-year run at the helm of the global tech giant he co-founded. Huang, 63, also gave up his seat on the board because of the scandal, AFP reported.

 

ALSO SEE: Global Leaders Heading to Asia for Talks on Trade, AI and Nukes

 

These developments followed a New York Times report alleging that the company founder had a second extramarital affair.

The scandal has sent shares of the multi-trillion dollar behemoth plunging. Nvidia shares were down as much as 13% in early trading on Wall Street following the announcement, with $800 billion wiped off the company’s valuation since the weekend.

The exit of Huang, a close informal adviser to President Donald Trump on AI, leaves Nvidia without its leather-jacket-clad leader at a crucial time for the sector.

Huang was a central figure in the revolution set off by the launch of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in 2022, with Nvidia’s powerful processors, once intended for video game graphics, becoming the crucial ingredient for building the AI models now spreading across the world.

Huang remains Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder, with a stake of about 3.6%, according to the company’s most recent filing. However, the stake gives him no special voting power, unlike founders at Meta or Google, who control their companies through super-voting shares.

For many in Silicon Valley, the dramatic departure will compare to that of Steve Jobs, who was pushed out of Apple by its board in 1985 and returned 12 years later to take the company to new heights.

 

Spy allegations

At the heart of the spy allegations is the race between the United States and China, with both superpowers trying to get ahead in an industry widely seen as the next industrial revolution.

The board said it had appointed Harvey Jones, a former head of chip design software firm Synopsys, as chair.

“The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption,” Jones said in a statement.

Kress said she was committed to “building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”

The scandal began with reports that Huang, who has been married to his wife Lori Huang for more than 40 years after meeting at university, was involved in an extramarital relationship.

Jensen Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, who was a senior executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. The two are not related.

US intelligence reportedly circulated a memo this spring alleging Alice Huang was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security.

Huang has spent years lobbying against curbs on sales of advanced AI chips to China, and US President Donald Trump last year cleared Nvidia’s H200 chips for export there over objections from Beijing’s critics in both parties.

Beijing, meanwhile, has rejected the spying allegations and claimed that the US was using spurious claims as a pretext to impose a technological ‘blockage’ on China.

“China’s technological progress is driven by independent innovation and open cooperation. The US side should stop fabricating such ‘spy’ narratives as a pretext for imposing a technological blockade,” foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular briefing on Thursday.

The rapidly unfolding story exploded after reports that Huang, who has been married to Lori Huang for over 40 years, was involved in an extramarital romance.

 

 

Alice Huang was among the attendees at a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei on May 22, 2025, during Computex, the island’s top tech expo.

At one point, Jensen Huang can be seen putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kisses him on the right cheek, press livestreams show, AFP reported.

She visited Taiwan a total of eight times in 2024 and 2025, a Taiwanese government minister said on Thursday.

Nvidia’s board had already announced on Sunday a probe of what it called reporting that Jensen Huang had been the target of a “foreign intelligence effort”.

Then came a New York Times report on Wednesday that the Nvidia co-founder was involved in a second extramarital affair, saying there was video evidence of the tech chief being affectionate with Nvidia’s vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell.

Powell, 48, has been a public face of Nvidia’s efforts to expand the chip technology into higher education and healthcare, and was speaking at a San Jose, California conference where they “were seen being affectionate at the hotel” by bystanders, the Times reported.

 

Code of conduct

The chip giant’s code of conduct tells associates to avoid conflicts of interest, and cites the example of “personal relationships”.

“We avoid situations where our actions might create a conflict – actual or potential – between our personal gain and our obligations to Nvidia”, the code says.

Nvidia’s bylaws require a majority of the 11 board directors to remove Huang as CEO. But he would retain his board seat, which could only be taken away by shareholders.

Huang has repeatedly avoided naming a successor when the question is brought up.

The New York Times earlier reported that the tech CEO has been called on by Congress to provide a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang.

As the artificial intelligence industry surge has spurred Nvidia’s stock prices to new heights, Huang has appeared at US President Donald Trump’s side at White House events, as recently as last month when he accepted a National Medal of Science from the Republican leader.

Huang was among the world’s most influential tech leaders – including Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg – who vowed to self-regulate AI against possible threats, as Trump rejected calls for government oversight and dismissed warnings the technology could wipe out humanity.

Nvidia shareholders filed a class action lawsuit against Huang and the AI chip maker for failing to disclose information about the relationship to investors.

Founded in 1993, Nvidia designs advanced components originally created to handle 3D visuals in video games, called Graphics Processing Units (GPUs).

Nvidia’s processors are mostly made by Taiwanese company TSMC, the world’s largest contract manufacturer of chips.

Nvidia is scheduled to release its quarterly results on November 17.

 

Indonesian political crisis

Meanwhile, in other Asian news, Indonesia’s vice president resigned Thursday, undone by a scandal over his high school diploma that has added to pressure on a government facing widespread dissatisfaction over the economy, graft and wildfires.

There had been repeated calls for Gibran Rakabuming Raka, 39, to step down following a Supreme Court ruling last month to annul his high school qualification, obtained abroad.

On Thursday, he submitted his resignation to President Prabowo Subianto and to parliament.

Prabowo told reporters he had accepted Gibran’s resignation “with a heavy heart” and praised him for acting “for a greater cause, for the interests of the nation, the state, and the people of Indonesia”.

“He certainly feels that he has pursued his education through an orderly process, but we all understand that the education system abroad is different from the education system in Indonesia,” the president said.

Indonesia’s vice president does not have many constitutionally defined powers apart from acting as the president’s representative at official events and taking over if his boss is incapacitated.

‘Political realignment’

Gibran’s downfall came after thousands of Indonesians took to the streets in recent weeks to protest economic hardship, graft, perceived authoritarianism and the government’s handling of months of devastating wildfires emitting toxic haze.

His exit is likely to complicate a loose governing alliance that includes the parties of Prabowo and of his predecessor Joko Widodo – Gibran’s father, who goes by Jokowi.

The resignation “marks a significant political realignment, but does not necessarily threaten government stability”, according to Khairul Fahmi, executive director of the Institute for Security and Strategic Studies (ISESS) think tank.

“Jokowi will retain political influence, but Gibran’s departure could reduce his network’s direct access to power. For Prabowo, this creates greater room to consolidate his leadership and pursue his own political agenda,” Khairul told AFP.

Two years into his term, Prabowo’s popularity has reached record lows.

Last week, Indonesian authorities arrested the former national police chief and three senior police officials for allegedly tapping the president’s telephone.

On Thursday, police said they were investigating possible treason.

Prabowo’s rise to power was widely credited to support from the popular Jokowi, who served two terms from 2014 to 2024.

The choice of Gibran as running mate strengthened ties between Prabowo’s Gerindra party and figures aligned to Jokowi, until then a political rival who had defeated Prabowo twice in presidential elections.

Under the alliance, Gibran and other Jokowi allies were appointed to key positions in the government of Prabowo, who is seen as close to the military while the police has traditionally been loyal to Jokowi.

Youngest-ever VP

Gibran became the youngest person ever to hold Indonesia’s vice presidency. Then, two years into his term, detractors went to court to challenge his high school certificate – a prerequisite for the job.

Gibran had completed his schooling in Singapore before going on to study for a marketing degree there.

When submitting his candidacy to the General Elections Commission (KPU) in 2024, he filed a certificate stating his overseas education was equivalent to a vocational high school in Indonesia.

Last month, however, Indonesia’s Supreme Court ruled to invalidate the document, prompting moves in parliament to unseat him.

Gibran has consistently defended his credentials. “If I didn’t graduate from high school, then I obviously wouldn’t have been able to go to college. I studied up to a bachelor’s degree in Singapore,” he has said.

Prabowo now has 14 days to submit two names from which parliament will have two months to pick Gibran’s replacement.

Researcher Arya Fernandes of Indonesia’s Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) told AFP Prabowo will likely seek “a candidate who is acceptable to all coalition members to avoid triggering divisions within the coalition” that includes Jokowi’s party.

“The vice-presidential candidate nominated by Prabowo could potentially become his running mate in 2029, or emerge as a political competitor. He will therefore carefully weigh the pros and cons of each potential nominee,” he said.

 

  • AFP with additional input and editing by Jim Pollard
